title: Two scales, one dose
spec: U13 · reconciling the Token Lens with the bench harness
intro: A drifting scale looks exactly like a working one. Weigh every call twice — the app's own receipt and the external harness — assert they agree, then use the same discipline to read a published 71.5x claim.
foot: Do it for real: python bench/run_campaign.py --modes naive,okf --questions Q3 --replay and compare against the Token Lens.

steps.title: The pharmacy weighs it twice
narrative: A compounding pharmacy weighs every dose on two different scales. Not because either is bad — because a scale that has drifted produces confident, plausible, wrong numbers, and disagreement is the cheapest detector that exists.

This repo ships two independent instruments over the same calls. The Token Lens is the app's own receipt: layer-by-layer accounting rendered next to the answer, plus a server-side correctness verdict. The harness is bench/run_campaign.py, which POSTs to /api/copilot/ask, grades the answer itself through bench/verify.py, and writes its own row. Neither reads the other's conclusion.
steps.youDo: Run one cell through the harness while watching the same question in the app.

steps.title: Assertion one — the layers must sum to the total
narrative: The first reconciliation is arithmetic, and it is the one that catches a broken seam fastest. Every receipt reports five layers and an input total; the total must equal the sum of the layers, for every cell, with no slack.

Take Q3 in okf: 65 + 102 + 0 + 0 + 19 = 186, which is exactly the input total the harness recorded. Run that check across all 100 cells of the shipped grid and the drift count is zero. This is the assertion that would have caught the response-shape seam failure this course hit during its own build — a harness reading a wrapper key that wasn't there, recording 100 cells of zeros, and only being noticed because a 0-token PASS is arithmetically impossible.

steps.title: Assertion two — two graders, one verdict
narrative: The second reconciliation is about judgement, not arithmetic. Every row carries verdict (the harness graded the answer text against the key) and backend_verdict (the server graded it independently). They must match on every cell. On the shipped grid, 100 cells, zero disagreements — and the runner prints a loud WARNING the moment that stops being true.

An instrument you trust because it has never complained is not an instrument. So prove the grader can fail before you believe it passing: bench/verify_selftest.py feeds it three planted wrong answers — a wrong threshold, a fabricated date of birth, a denial with the wrong reason — and the selftest only passes if the grader catches all three.
The rule when the two disagree is uncomfortable and non-negotiable: you stop trusting both until you know why. One of them is wrong and you do not yet know which.
steps.youDo: Run python bench/verify_selftest.py first, every time — a grader that cannot fail cannot grade.

steps.title: The canary that has no fallback
narrative: Reconciliation catches instruments that disagree. It does not catch instruments that agree and are both wrong — which is what happens when the infrastructure underneath a whole arm fails politely.

The knowledge-graph course paid for this twice: two complete campaigns measured a "graph arm" whose MCP server had been silently crashing. File-tool fallbacks made the failure invisible; the arm kept answering, the numbers looked plausible, and the conclusion ("the graph doesn't help much") was confidently wrong. The rule that came out of it: always run one arm with no fallback.

In MedFlow that arm is okf. It answers only from canonical concept files. Break the concept store and okf fails loudly on the next question instead of quietly degrading into naive behaviour — which is precisely why it is also the arm whose numbers you can trust most.

before.title: BEFORE — every arm has a fallback

view.text: The concept store is down. The arm falls back to reading the domain dump, answers correctly, and posts a token number that describes a completely different mechanism. Two campaigns later, someone writes "curated context provides only marginal benefit" in a report.

after.title: AFTER — one arm refuses to improvise

view.text: okf has no fallback path. The concept store is down, so the arm errors on question one, the campaign stops, and you fix an infrastructure bug instead of publishing a finding about it. A canary is not redundancy — it is deliberately removed redundancy.

steps.title: The anatomy of 71.5x
narrative: Now apply the same scepticism to a published number. The famous 71.5x token reduction for structural code context is real — as a ceiling case: one favourable corpus, one favourable query shape, and a baseline that dumped whole files. Independent replications of the same tool class land between 6.8x and 49x, and on some stacks it loses outright.

Nothing was faked. What happened is a quantity-class swap: a mechanical floor, or someone else's session, quoted as though it were a prediction about your stack. All three are correct answers to different questions, and only the third is a forecast.

So place your own numbers in their class before you compare anything. This bench's okf arm reaches 9.1x over naive on medians and 7.1x for the router — respectable numbers that would look feeble next to 71.5x and are not on the same axis as it, because these are graded against an answer key and that one was not.

steps.title: Publish the conditions with the number
narrative: The last discipline is the cheapest and the most often skipped: every headline number travels with the conditions that produced it. Ten questions. One corpus. Deterministic replay, so repetitions would be theatre — the median-of-three rule becomes mandatory the moment you record live, because identical fresh sessions have been measured varying by 2x.

And report the summary that matches the claim. "7.1x" is a median over single questions; across the full ten-question session the router spends 5,644 tokens against naive's 16,948, which is 3.0x. Both are true, neither is the other, and a scorecard that prints only the flattering one has quietly become the thing this module is about.
steps.youDo: Take any number you are about to publish and write its four conditions next to it: corpus, question mix, baseline, and source label.
